headline: Yakuwari is 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) plus 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).

sources.quote: From 役 (yaku, “service, work, role”) and 割り (wari), the noun form of 割る (waru, “to divide”).

examples.ja: 私の役割は何ですか。
examples.en: Where do I come in?

examples.ja: 彼はその革命で積極的な役割をした。
examples.en: He played an active part in the revolution.

headline: Moeru is from the classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu), by way of moju and mojeru.

sources.quote: /moju/ → /mojeru/ → /moeru/
From classical verb 燃ゆ (moyu).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.

examples.ja: 木が燃える。
examples.en: Wood burns.

examples.ja: 火は燃える。
examples.en: Fire burns.

meaning: to cover, to hide, to conceal
headline: Ōu is the Old Japanese verb 覆ふ (opu, “cover from above”) plus ふ (-fu), which expresses repetition or ongoing state.

sources.quote: /opu pu/ → /opopu/ → /ofofu/ → */owou/ → /oːu/
From the Old Japanese verb 覆(お)ふ (opu, “cover from above”) + ふ (-fu, auxiliary verb modifier, expressing repetition or ongoing state).

examples.ja: 町は雪で覆われていた。
examples.en: The city was blanketed with snow.

examples.ja: 空は雲で覆われている。
examples.en: The sky is covered with clouds.

headline: Tō, “tower”, abbreviates 卒塔婆 (sotoba), a transliteration of Sanskrit stūpa, “heap”.

sources.quote: /tapu/ → /taɸu/ → */tawu/ → /tau/ → /tɔː/ → /toː/
From Middle Chinese 塔 (MC thap, “tower, pagoda, spire”).
An abbreviation for 卒塔婆 (sotoba, sotōba), a transliteration of Sanskrit स्तूप (stūpa, “heap”).

examples.ja: あれは塔です。
examples.en: That is a pagoda.

examples.ja: 遠くに塔が見えた。
examples.en: We saw the tower in the distance.

headline: Su, “nest”, is found in the Kojiki of 712, from Proto-Japonic *su.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Found in the Kojiki of 712, and included in the Man'yōshū with the phonetic man'yōgana spelling 須 (su). In turn, from Proto-Japonic *su.

examples.ja: 蜘蛛は巣を張る。
examples.en: A spider weaves a web.

examples.ja: 鳥は木に巣を作る。
examples.en: Birds make their nests in trees.

headline: Chii is from Middle Chinese 地位, first cited in Japanese in the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 地位 (MC dijH hwijH). First cited in Japanese to a text from the mid-1200s, so possibly a learned borrowing from Chinese 地位 (dìwèi).

examples.ja: 彼は地位に満足だ。
examples.en: He enjoys his position.

examples.ja: 彼はよい地位を得た。
examples.en: He got a good appointment.

headline: Sensu is first attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.

sources.quote: Ultimately from Middle Chinese 扇子.
First attested in Japanese in the Taiheiki of the late 1300s.

examples.ja: 犬が腕時計と扇子を食った。
examples.en: The dog ate a watch and a Japanese fan.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Hitomi is likely 人 (hito, “person”) plus 見 (mi, “see”): one's own reflection in someone else's eyes.

sources.quote: Likely 人(ひと) (hito, “person”) + 見(み) (mi, “see”), in reference to one's own reflection when staring into someone else's eyes. Compare Latin pūpilla, of the same derivation.

examples.ja: 瞳は日のあたる所では収縮する。
examples.en: The pupils of the eyes contract in sunlight.

examples.ja: あなたの瞳に、吸い込まれそう！
examples.en: I feel like I'm being drawn into your eyes.

headline: Urusai is probably 心 (uru, “heart, mind”) plus 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”): something so overwhelming that one feels pressured.

sources.quote: Probably originally a compound of 心 (uru, “heart, mind”, vowel-shifted from regular reading ura, cognate with 裏 (ura, “the behind or inside of something”)) + 狭し (sashi, “tight; narrow”, Classical and Old Japanese, cognate and synonym of modern 狭い (semai)), from the sense that something is so overwhelming that one feels pressured to yield or submit in some way.

The earliest texts used this word to mean something more like "overwhelmed by how completely thorough something is (in a positive sense), or by how excessive and repetitive something is (in a negative sense)". Over time, the term was used less and less in a positive sense, and the focus from the late Heian period gradually became a negative sense of oppression and annoyance from something troublesome, repetitive, or overwhelming. Usage then shifted further, such that the term described not the speaker's own internal state, but rather the troublesome quality of the cause of the emotional response.
First cited to works from the early 900s.

meaning: to change, to alter, to vary
headline: Kaeru, “to change”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) pattern.
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 下(しも)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo nidan katsuyō, “lower bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 下(しも)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (shimo ichidan katsuyō, “lower monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -eru.
Cognate with 替(か)える (kaeru), 代(か)える (kaeru) and 換(か)える (kaeru).

examples.ja: 彼は話題を変えた。
examples.en: He changed the topic of conversation.

examples.ja: 彼は仕事を変えた。
examples.en: He changed his job.

headline: Oba, an aunt, is likely 小 (o-, “small, young”) plus 母 (ha, “mother”), as 叔父 (oji) is 小 plus 父.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Attested in a text from 701. In turn, reconstructed as descending from Proto-Japonic *wonpa.
Likely a compound of 小 (o-, “small, young”) + 母 (ha, “mother”). Compare 叔父 (oji, “uncle”), also likely from 小 (o-) + 父 (chi, “father”).

headline: Chūshajō is 駐車 (chūsha, “(car) parking”) plus 場 (-jō, “place”).

sources.quote: 駐車(ちゅうしゃ) (chūsha, “(car) parking”) + 場(じょう) (-jō, “place”)

examples.ja: 駐車場はありますか。
examples.en: Is there a parking lot?

examples.ja: その駐車場は無料だ。
examples.en: The parking lot is free of charge.

headline: Tadaima is short for 只今、帰りました (tadaima, kaerimashita), “I'm back right now”.

sources.quote: Short of 只(ただ)今(いま)、帰(かえ)りました (tadaima, kaerimashita, “I'm back right now”).

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Mukai is the continuative stem of 向かう (mukau, “to face”).

sources.quote: The 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 向(む)かう (mukau, “to face”).

examples.ja: 店は銀行の向かいにある。
examples.en: The shop is across from the bank.

examples.ja: ちょうど教会の向かいです。
examples.en: It's just across the street from the church.

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: In hōtai, 包 is a daiyōji replacing 繃.

sources.quote: 包 is a daiyōji replacing 繃.

examples.ja: 包帯をしなさい。
examples.en: Apply a bandage.

examples.ja: 彼女は傷口に包帯をした。
examples.en: She applied a bandage to the wound.

headline: Fushi was pusi in Old Japanese, attested in 794 as 布之.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese 節 (pusi); attested in the Shin'yaku Kegonkyō Ongi Shiki of 794 as 布之. In turn, from Proto-Japonic *pusi. Possibly derived from Old Japanese 節 (pu).

examples.ja: 彼には加古川の人を軽蔑しているふしがある。
examples.en: He seems to hold people from Kakogawa in contempt.

headline: Hizuke is 日 (hi, “day”) plus 付け (-zuke, “fixing, attaching”).

sources.quote: 日(ひ) (hi, “day”) + 付(づ)け (-zuke, “fixing, attaching”)

examples.ja: 私は会議の日付を忘れた。
examples.en: I forgot the date of the meeting.

examples.ja: 彼女は日付を数字で書いた。
examples.en: She wrote the date in numeric form.

meaning: to see off; to escort; to let pass
headline: Miokuru is 見 (mi, “seeing”) plus 送る (okuru, “to send”).

sources.quote: 見(み) (mi, “seeing”, 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 見(み)る (miru, “to see”)) + 送(おく)る (okuru, “to send”)

examples.ja: 空港で彼女を見送った。
examples.en: We saw her off at the airport.

examples.ja: 彼を空港で見送りました。
examples.en: I saw him off at the airport.

headline: Nobiru, “to be prolonged”, is from the classical upper bigrade verb のぶ, cognate with 伸びる (nobiru).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ. Cognate with Japanese 伸(の)びる (nobiru).

headline: Uranau is from 裏 (ura, “back, inside”) or 心 (ura, “heart”), plus なふ (nau, verb modifier).

sources.quote: From either 裏(うら) (ura, “back, inside”) or 心(うら) (ura, “heart”, by extension, "inner feelings"), and なふ (nau, verb modifier).

examples.ja: 私は運勢を占ってもらった。
examples.en: I had my fortune told.

meaning: to extend, to make progress, to grow
headline: This nobiru, written 伸, shares its classical verb のぶ (nobu) with 延びる (nobiru).

sources.quote: From the classical upper bigrade verb(バ行上二段活用) のぶ (nobu). Cognate with Japanese 延(の)びる (nobiru).
Development

Natural progression from Old and Classical Japanese 上(かみ)二(に)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami nidan katsuyō, “upper bigrade conjugation”) verbs ending in -u to modern Japanese 上(かみ)一(いち)段(だん)活(かつ)用(よう) (kami ichidan katsuyō, “upper monograde conjugation”) verbs ending in -iru.

examples.ja: 髪が伸びてきた。
examples.en: My hair has grown out.

examples.ja: 彼は過労で伸びている。
examples.en: He has been exhausted from overwork.

headline: Totemo is a clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”); the sense “very” is a later shift, first attested around 1910-1920.

sources.quote: Clipping of とてもかくても (“no matter how, not at all”), used with negative verbs. The sense "very, exceedingly" is a shift from the earlier sense of "no matter how", and was first attested around 1910-1920. Compare 全然.

headline: Yorokobi is the continuative stem of 喜ぶ (yorokobu, “to be pleased, delighted”).

sources.quote: 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 喜(よろこ)ぶ (yorokobu, “to be pleased, delighted”).

examples.ja: 喜びでわくわくした。
examples.en: I jumped for joy.

examples.ja: 喜びが彼の顔に出た。
examples.en: His joy showed on his face.

headline: Kyū ni is 急 (kyū, “sudden”) plus に (ni, oblique particle).

sources.quote: From 急(きゅう) (kyū, “sudden”) + に (ni, oblique particle).

examples.ja: 彼は急に居直った。
examples.en: He changed his attitude suddenly.

examples.ja: 車は急に左折した。
examples.en: The car cut to the left.

headline: Suruto is する (suru, “to do”) plus と (to): literally “when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]”.

sources.quote: From する (suru, “to do”) + と (to, “when, whenever”, temporal particle). Literally, "when doing [whatever came before], then [whatever comes after]".

examples.ja: するとあなたは幸せでしょう。
examples.en: Then you will be happy.

examples.ja: すると、たまたま少女のおばあちゃんが通りかかる。
examples.en: Along comes the grandmother and sees her granddaughter.

meaning: to return, to come back; to turn over
headline: Kaeru, “to return”, is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapyaru.

sources.quote: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kapyaru.

headline: Nikui is cognate with 憎む (nikumu, “to hate”).

sources.quote: From Old Japanese. Cognate with 憎む (nikumu, “to hate”), 難い (-nikui, “difficult [to do]”, verb suffix).

examples.ja: 憎い憎いは可愛いの裏。
examples.en: Hatred is the other side of cuteness.

examples.ja: かわいさ余って憎さ百倍。
examples.en: The greatest hate springs from the greatest love.

headline: Daga is だ (da, “is, are”, copula) plus が (ga).

sources.quote: Phrase consisting of だ (da, “is, are”, copula) + が (ga, nominative particle, also used contrastively after verbs).
が is also used after verbs in this same way to indicate “the previous statement is the case, but...”

examples.ja: だがすでに、賽は投げられた。
examples.en: However, the die had already been cast.

examples.ja: だが、ビルは「バナナ」と言った。
examples.en: However, Bill said "banana."

headline: Sono is そ, the distal demonstrative root of Old Japanese, plus の (no).

sources.quote: ⟨so₂ no₂⟩ → */sənə/ → /sono/
From Old Japanese そ, distal demonstrative root, with の (no) added to form the ordinary adnominal form 'that', as in 'that word', as opposed to the pronoun それ (sore).

pos: noun or participle which takes the aux. verb suru
headline: In chūmon, 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.

sources.quote: 注 is a daiyōji replacing 註.

examples.ja: ご注文をどうぞ。
examples.en: May I have your order, please?

examples.ja: 注文の品が届いた。
examples.en: The items which you ordered arrived.

pos: nouns which may take the genitive case particle 'no'
headline: Saitei is 最 (sai-, “most”) plus 低 (tei, “low”).

sources.quote: From 最(さい) (sai-, “most”) + 低(てい) (tei, “low”).

examples.ja: あの映画、最低！
examples.en: That movie stinks!

examples.ja: 費用は最低一万円です。
examples.en: The expense is 10000 yen at lowest.
